newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. agency warns Hutu refugees could die in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. agency warns Hutu refugees could die in Zaire.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency warned on Saturday many Rwandan Hutu refugees trapped in the Zaire jungle would die unless aid workers provided urgently needed food, water and medicine.

Tens of thousands of Rwandan Hutus are stranded in dense jungle near a railway line south of Kisangani, Zaire's third city, which fell on March 15 to rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL).
At least 500 have been buried since arriving at Ubilo, 82 km (51 miles) south of the city on March 16, according to the Zairean Red Cross, and unburied bodies litter the surrounding land.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said it was negotiating with the rebels over a plan to give the refugees short term aid consisting of food, water and medicine and was devising plans to return them to Rwanda.
"Without the crucial elements (of this plan) the people will start dying in very large numbers. Many have already died," Filippo Grandi, head of UNHCR in Goma told Reuters.
"There is a risk of serious epidemics if we don't bring water very quickly," Grandi said.
The Zairean rebels who have seized control of a quarter of the country since last October are pushing towards the second city Lubumbashi, capital of Shaba region, and diamond-rich Mbuji Mayi.
Negotiations between the AFDL and envoys of ailing president Mobutu Sese Seko would start early next week probably in South Africa, according to an Alliance spokesman.
The U.N. World Food Programme, UNHCR and the Zairean Red Cross carried the first train-load of 120 tonnes of food and medicine to the refugees on Thursday and Friday.
The refugees lining the railway line as the train approached made a pitiful sight.
Emaciated refugees, some almost skeletal, were attempting to walk towards aid at Kisangani while those too weak to start the trek lay dead and dying within the abandoned Ubilo camp.
More than a million Hutus fled camps on the Rwandan and Burundian border last October and November at the start of a campaign by rebels fighting the Zairean army.

Around 600,000 returned to Rwanda in November via Goma but hundreds of thousands more fled west into the jungle among them members of the former Rwandan government army and extremist Interahamwe militia held responsible for massacres during the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.
Since then the refugees -- now begging to return home -- have set up a series of makeshift camps and fled before the rebel advance in a trek that has hampered relief efforts.
UNHCR said it was appealing to donors for money to fly the most vulnerable refugees direct to the Rwandan capital Kigali from Kisangani at a rate of up to 2,000 per day.
The rest would be made strong enough and then returned to Rwanda overland by truck, barge and on foot.
"This is the land option, but it means that they have to go through Kisangani which the Alliance is refusing. This is the negotiation we are having right now," Grandi said.
The rebels, who include many Tutsi fighters, attacked and killed at least 100 of the armed refugees in two incidents last week, according to residents.
